HDL carries dietary fat from the intestine
LDL is protective and HDL is harmful
h: Which one is called “good” cholesterol, and why?
w: LDL delivers cholesterol to tissues (high levels linked to plaque); HDL returns excess cholesterol to the liver.

q: After a fatty meal, dietary triacylglycerols leave the intestine packed in which lipoprotein?
h: This is the largest, least dense lipoprotein.
w: Intestinal cells package absorbed fat into chylomicrons, which enter the lymph and then the blood.

q: Which of these is NOT a ketone body?
h: Ketone bodies are made from acetyl CoA in the liver.
w: The three ketone bodies are acetoacetate, β-hydroxybutyrate and acetone. Pyruvate is the product of glycolysis.

q: The liver makes ketone bodies during fasting, but it does not use them. Which tissues use them for energy?
c: heart, muscle and (after several days) the brain
no tissue; they are only excreted
h: Ketone bodies are fuel sent out from the liver.
w: Ketone bodies are exported to heart, skeletal muscle and the brain (once it adapts); the liver lacks the enzyme needed to use them.

q: Fatty acid synthesis (lipogenesis) adds carbons to the growing chain two at a time from
c: malonyl CoA (as malonyl ACP), releasing CO<sub>2</sub>
h: A three-carbon unit is added and one carbon leaves as CO<sub>2</sub>.
w: Each turn adds a two-carbon unit from malonyl ACP; its third carbon leaves as CO2.

q: Which hormone promotes lipogenesis and fat storage after a carbohydrate-rich meal?
h: Which hormone signals the fed state?
w: Insulin promotes fatty acid synthesis and storage of triacylglycerols; glucagon and epinephrine promote fat breakdown.

q: Transamination enzymes (such as ALT and AST) require which coenzyme?
h: The coenzyme carries the amino group between molecules.
w: Every transaminase uses pyridoxal phosphate (vitamin B6) to carry the amino group.

q: ALT is a transamination enzyme found mainly inside liver cells. A blood test shows a high level of ALT. What is the best explanation?
c: injured liver cells are leaking ALT into the blood
the liver is making extra ALT to speed up transamination
a high-protein meal raised the blood ALT
h: ALT works inside cells. How would it get into the blood?
w: ALT normally stays inside liver cells. When the cells are damaged, their contents leak into the blood, so a high ALT signals liver injury.

q: In which organ is urea made?
h: Urea is made in one organ and excreted by another.
w: The urea cycle runs in the liver; the kidneys then excrete urea in the urine.

q: Urea is made in the liver and removed from the blood by the kidneys. A patient with kidney failure has a high blood urea nitrogen (BUN). Why?
c: the kidneys cannot excrete the urea that the liver keeps making
the liver makes too much glucose
the patient is not eating protein
h: Where is urea made, and where does it leave the body?
w: The liver keeps producing urea, but failing kidneys cannot clear it, so urea accumulates in the blood.

q: In severe liver failure, blood ammonia rises and the patient becomes confused (hepatic encephalopathy). Why does ammonia build up?
c: the failing liver cannot convert ammonium ion into urea
the kidneys excrete too much urea
h: Which liver pathway disposes of nitrogen?
w: Ammonium from amino acid breakdown is normally turned into urea in the liver; when the urea cycle fails, ammonia accumulates and is toxic to the brain.

q: Which person is most likely to be in positive nitrogen balance (taking in more nitrogen than is excreted)?
c: a person on a very low-protein diet
h: Positive balance means protein is being built up.
w: Growth, pregnancy and recovery build new protein, so a growing child retains nitrogen: positive nitrogen balance.

q: A patient with extensive burns breaks down muscle protein faster than it is replaced. What is her nitrogen balance?
c: nitrogen balance does not apply to protein
h: Is she excreting more nitrogen than she takes in?
w: Net protein breakdown means more nitrogen is excreted (as urea) than eaten: negative nitrogen balance.

q: An amino acid whose carbon skeleton is degraded to pyruvate or a citric acid cycle intermediate is called
h: Which of those products can be turned into glucose?
w: Pyruvate and cycle intermediates can be made into glucose, so the amino acid is glucogenic.

q: In phenylketonuria (PKU), phenylalanine hydroxylase is missing, so phenylalanine cannot be converted to tyrosine. What is the treatment? (Phenylalanine is both glucogenic and ketogenic.)
c: a low-phenylalanine diet, avoiding aspartame, beginning in infancy
h: The goal is to keep phenylalanine from building up.
w: A lifelong low-phenylalanine diet prevents the build-up that damages the developing brain; aspartame contains phenylalanine and carries a warning label.

q: Glutamate undergoes oxidative deamination in the liver. Besides NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>, what are the products?
h: The amino group leaves and the carbon becomes a C=O; NAD<sup>+</sup> is the oxidizing agent.
w: Glutamate dehydrogenase removes the amino group as NH4+, leaving α-ketoglutarate, and reduces NAD+ to NADH.
